regions.text: INTRODUCTION

The volume herewith presented to patrons embodies the 19'22
edition of R. L Polk & Co.'s Gary City Directory. The work repre-
sents a careful canvass of the city and its immediately adjoining en-
virons: also an assemblage of all vital information concerning the
social, commercial. linancial and industrial interests and activities
of the municipality. The publishers have given the publication the
benefit and advantage of their complete modern organization, de-
voted exclusively to the production of Directories. Their imprint
on the greatest of Directories attests the quality and completeness
of their work. The Directory has been carefully compijed and the
several departments have been arranged in such order as to render
easy access to each feature Of the Directory. The standard estab-
lished in previous editions is fully maintained in this issue, and toe
volume will be found to fully measure up to and meet the need, and
requirements of patrons. The Notable Statistical review forming
part of This Imroduction is inipressive as showing the adv;'nce:;
made by Gan- in civies, finance and industry.

Gary was founded in 1906 on the shore of Lake Michigan, on
the northern edge of Indiana, a few miles southeast of Chicago, as
the seat of a colossal industrial unit-The Indiana (now Illinois)
Steel Company, a subsidiary of the United States Steel Corporation.
The site was named for Hon. Elbert H. Gary, an eminent lawyer,
and Chairman of the Corporation.
Where sixteen years age were sand dunes and many of the
characteristics as well as the environments of a frontier town, now
stands a beautiful city with parks in place of the dunes. a vast steel
indtistry and some lesser ones calling for the energies of thousands
of workers, and a population housed in modern residences. The
great mills, some of which are open-hearth furnaces, are responsi-
ble for its location. Three-fourths of the iron used in the United
States comes from the Lake Superior region. From Duluth to Gary
is a broad waterway giving the cheapest transportation possible.
Gary, therefore, is situated conveniently as regards ore.
Ore alone. however. is of no practical value. To work it up into
useful forms. coke is needed. and coke implies coal. South and east
from Gary there are vast coal regions. The city may be said to lie
half way between the two most necessary things for manufacturing
steel cheaply in great quantities: it is midway between the coal felds
and ore deposits, and for one of these essentials it has water trans-
portation. Limestone, too, which cleans much of the impurities out
of the molten metal. is in demand for the blast furnaces todai·. A
layer of coke. a layer of lime, a layer of ore is the rule in smelters
Gary is near great areas of limestone.
Judge Gary, in his official capacity as Chairman of the United
States Steel Corporation. publicly stated in a speech at Duluth that
steel products could be made in Gary 38 per cent cheaper than in
Duluth and 25 per cent cheaper than in Pittsburgh: that Gary.
owiNK to its unsurpassed facilities for assembling the raw material
and the distribution of the finished product . together with that rare
combination of other things which are necessary in the manufac-
ture of steel, including the wonderful efficiency of its up-to-date
plant. is the place of all places in the world where steel can be pro-
duced at the lowest cost.
In the output of steel the Gary mills have broken all records
since the world began.
This is why the United States Steel Corporation has poured out
inal~>· millions of dollars in erecting its plants in Gary rather than
in Pennsylvania or Ohio: this is why Gary has grown so tremen-
dously in so short a time. and why Gary must continue to grow
rapidly, until as a steel center, the Gary region overtops all rivals.
To the thousands now buying and building their own homes in
Gary, Judge Gary's speech will give renewed confidence that the
property into which they are putting their savings is located in a

city which is destined to be the greatest steel manufacturing center
in the world, and in which values are bound to increase with the
development of the industries.
Both the carload and the personal additions to Gary are in-
creasing. With labor, raw material and markets for products right
at hand in greater quantity and convenience than is possible else-
where because of the natural geographical conditions of the city’s
position, what is there for steelmen to do but come to Gary with as
little delay as possible? The newest ideas in steel manufacture are
already in evidence here. The natural facilities are incomparable.
To work against, or in competition with such conditions in any
place outside of the “Calumet” district can hardly be considered a
hopeful prospect.
Those who chose the site for Gary chose it because it was THE
site. They had the land’s surface of the whole world to choose from.
The one place upon the earth that met the conditions which the
demands for the highest efficiency in the production of manufac-
tured steel called for, was the place that the city of Gary now occu-
pies. Being the best place for the world’s best organized business,
will Gary grow? What else can it do?
What land sold for in the beginning of Gary, and what it sells
for now, shows an appreciation most gratifying to early purchasers,
but still greater appreciations are coming. They come because cities
like Gary, and Gary probably at the head of its class, grow continu-
ously by assimilation.
To visit Gary and see by personal inspection what natural con-
ditions have made possible here, and to observe how inevitable the
city’s growth has been because of the natural facilities that obtain
here, is to become convinced that Gary is substantial and secure.
Gary is not a speculation, it is not a clever guess, itis a fact. Itisa
fact of large dimensions, which grows larger daily because the city
has three first-class advantages. It is near the great essentials for
commercial prosperity. It has at hand the trinity of things needful,
sources of supply, markets for its goods and labor.
Gary is in the midst of the “Calumet” region, which region,
from the manufacturing and distributing viewpoint, is probably the
most extraordinary that this world has seen. Not only is Gary in
the heart of this region, but it is becoming the most important fac-
tor in its tremendous manufacturing and distributing energies.

FIRE DEPARTMENT
Gary for its age and size has one of the finest organizations of
any city for fire protection: the department has its headquarters in
the City Hall. There are six stations. 81 men: 4 combination hose
and chemical autos: 3 hose wagons, 2 hook and ladder trucks and 1
chief's car: the equipment is all motor-driven. There are 660
hydrants. The value of buildings and lots is $78,864.68, and of the
apparatus and other equipment, $90,920.95.

The city is lighted by 548 arc lamps. Broadway is brilliantly
illuminated with white-globe clustered lights over its rapidly grow-
ing length, distinguishing Gary as one of the best lighted cities in
the country.
The metropolitan boulevard lighting system is extraordinary.
The main thoroughfare corners have four posts capped with white-
globed clusters, and every fifty feet between corners a post with
three cluster lights. Gas is manufactured for heating, lighting and
cooking and for use in industries; 54 miles of mains have been laid.
The gas plant will accommodate a population of 250,000.

The map shows the convenience to market which Gary affords
for manufactured pruducts. Six trunk lines of railway traverse the
city with two belt lines connecting all roads entering Chicago dis-
trict, besides several lines such as the Gary and Interurban, South
Shore and the interurban to Crown Point, Valparaiso, Hobart. etc.,
not to mention the Elgin, Joliet and Eastern R. R., which does not
carry passengers but which connects with every freight road run-
ning out of Chicago. There are flve city and interurban lines with
30.12 miles of trackage on the city lines.
WATER 11()RKA
The capacity of the present plant of the Gary Heat, Light &
Water Co. is 38.000.000 gallons: daily average number of gallons
pumped is 4.300.000; during the dry. hot summer months the con-
sumption demand is at the rate of 18,000,000 gallons per day: the
pumping units are in duplicate; miles of water mains laid. 65.
Water is free to lawn owners by way of encouraging beautiful home
yards.
THE (:18¥ CHAPIBER OF ((l,1,11;RCE
The Gary Chamber of Commerce is an organization of business
interests, organized along business lines and operated under busi-
ness principles. It was reorganized into a modern Chamber of
Commerce February 1st. 1922. and its constitution and by-laws are
identically the same as the constitution and bi-laws that proved so
highly successful in other live cities in this country.
This organization is located at 19 East 6th Ave., with a Seere-
tary in charge whose duty it is to render every service and informa-
tion regarding our city and surrounding territories both to our citi-
zens and all visitors.
Mr. E. A. Warner is Secretary and Manager and the Board of
Directors consists of the following members: H. L Arnold. C. D.
Baker, H. J. Curtis. R. M. Davis. W. F. Hodges, R. O. Johnson, C. R.
Kuss, W. L. Plew. F. R. Schaaf. J. R. Snyder, P. H. Stevens, D. F.

has achieved success in extending the commercial interests of the
city. One of its principal purposes is to bring the citizens of the
community together in real co-operative effort to comprise all dif-
ferences of effort and to work harmoniously for community ad-
vancement.
DIRECTORY LIBRARY
A library of City Directories has been installed by the publish-
ers in the rooms of the Gary Chamber of Commerce at 19 E. 6th av.
for the free use of the public. As the latest Directories are issued
they will be added to the Library, thereby keeping it up-to-date from
year to year. We extend a cordial invitation to each and every one
to make frequent use of this Library and to consult the Directories
on file as often as desired when information in regard to any indi-
vidual, firm, corporation, or institution located in other cities is
desired.
MUNICIPAL PUBLICITY
ADVERTISING GARY
An important function of the Directory is to set forth the char-
acteristics and advantages of the city as a place of residence, as a
business location, as an industrial site and as an educational center.
The Directory acts as a mirror, reflecting all that is noteworthy in
the city in the above respects. In order to spread this information
regarding the city broadcast over the country the publishers place
copies of this issue of the Directory in Directory Libraries which are
maintained in all of the larger cities in the country where they are
readily available for reference use by the public. There they serve as
perpetual advertisements of Gary for business men the country over
